content.content:
`deccy remove <id>` refuses while any open record names the node, and the refusal names each such draft by its handle; a landed record does not block. The guard is a precondition on the removal that already exists, not a second verb and not a flag over it: `remove` abandons a node's change only when its preconditions hold, refusing otherwise and naming what stopped it (stnqmzuw), and this adds one more condition to that same refusal surface (myprwuxt).

The condition is asked of the records that name the node, and of nothing else. A record names exactly one target node (owyntkvw), so the question is one comparison per record — the record's target against the id the caller gave — and the answer does not rest on the node set: a record is not a node, is not listed with the nodes, carries no change and is not validated as one (owyntkvw), so nothing in the graph attests that a draft exists, and the scan for dependants that D14 fixes (stnqmzuw) cannot see a draft at all. The records are found where they are kept: by scanning `.deccy/work/` and taking each document named by its handle as one record (twpvqstu). There is no key to look a node up by — the record is keyed by its handle and the target node is one of its references (owyntkvw) — so no path names "the drafts of this node", and the directory's contents are the whole of the lookup (twpvqstu). Nor is the lookup confined to the caller's own workspace: the records sit in one registry for the repository (twpvqstu), and the workspace on a record is a reference to where its draft is written rather than the record's scope (owyntkvw), so a draft made in another workspace blocks exactly as one made here does.

Of the records that name the node, only the open ones block. The state is the landing fact — `open` is the record of a draft that has not landed, `landed` the record of one that has (vkkwusty) — so "has not landed" is exactly the condition the guard enforces, and it is read off the state rather than kept in a second bookkeeping of which drafts still matter. A landed record is retained and sits in the same directory at the same handle, so a scan taken at the removal finds it as surely as it finds the open ones (twpvqstu); it is passed over for what it says, not for being absent. Retention is what makes that exclusion necessary rather than convenient: a landed record is never deleted (vkkwusty), so read as a claim it would block every later removal of that node for the rest of its life, and the node would be out of the abandonment D7 fixes (myprwuxt) for good. The landed state is also terminal — `landed` has nowhere to go (vkkwusty) — so a record that passes the filter now will not arrive later as open, and the guard's answer does not depend on when it is asked.

The refusal names each open draft by its handle. The handle is the draft's identity and the only thing that picks it out (owyntkvw), so it is what a caller can carry to the landing that clears the refusal, and what tells the several drafts of one node apart — the node id cannot, because every one of them names it (owyntkvw). The workspace is not what the refusal names: it is one of the record's references and says where the draft is written, not which draft it is (owyntkvw). No alias is offered and no flag lifts the refusal (stnqmzuw): the answer changes when a record's state does, which is to say when the draft lands (vkkwusty).

The guard is answered before anything is abandoned. Removal abandons the named node's change and, with it, the node's own gates (myprwuxt), and no later landing undoes that: once the change is abandoned the node the draft names is gone with it, and the draft has nothing left to land into. So the open record has to stop the removal where removal can still be refused — before the bracket, alongside the refusals D14 and D7 already ask there (stnqmzuw, myprwuxt) — and that is the same shape those two have rather than a new one: the verb refuses while something stands in the way, names what stands, and abandons nothing. An invocation with no open record naming the node passes this guard and goes on to the rest of the removal exactly as it did before.

Against those two refusals the guard neither replaces nor narrows anything. D14 refuses a node that something depends on, naming the dependants, with no aliases (stnqmzuw); D7 abandons the named change and, with it, the node's own gates (myprwuxt). Both are asked as they were, and this node adds a third answer of the same kind: refused, with the open drafts named. The three are answered in the order removal already keeps — the dependants, then the node's other preconditions, then the abandonment — so the draft guard is asked after the dependant refusal: a node that is both depended on and drafted is refused naming its dependants, exactly as D14 has it, and the drafts are named once nothing depends on the node (stnqmzuw, myprwuxt). Answered the other way the guard would answer in the dependants' place and leave their names unsaid, which D14 does not allow (stnqmzuw); answered here, every name the caller is owed survives, and the cost is only that a call clearing both draws two refusals rather than one. Nothing about a draft's existence changes what the dependence check finds, and nothing about the dependence check changes which drafts are open.

The guard reads the id the caller named and no other. A gate abandoned after it goes with the gated, and no invocation names that gate, so no record is consulted here about the gate's own drafts (myprwuxt). What a landed record means once its target has been removed, what a scan does with a record it cannot read, and whether a draft is ever discarded rather than landed are not settled by this node (twpvqstu, vkkwusty).

These clauses are one commitment: the answer is read off the registry, at the open records, by the target they name, and named back by handle, before any change is abandoned. Take away the scan and the drafts would have to be found by a key that does not exist (owyntkvw); take away the state filter and a landed record would block the node for good (vkkwusty); take away the target field and the scan could not pick these records out from every other draft (owyntkvw); take away the handle and the refusal would name nothing a caller can act on (owyntkvw); take away the placement before the abandonment and the guard would arrive too late to be one (myprwuxt).
content.rationale:
The guard is a precondition added to a verb that already refuses, so its shape is D14's refusal-with-names rather than an error or a flag: the caller is told what stands in the way and can act on it, and no alias is introduced (stnqmzuw). D7's removal stays the thing being guarded rather than being re-decided — the change is still abandoned, its paths still released, its own gates still taken with it (myprwuxt) — and nothing here chooses a new verb or a second invocation form.

What the guard can read is fixed by where the drafts are. A record is one JSON document under `.deccy/work/` named by its handle, and the directory's contents are the whole list of records: there is no index beside them and nothing else enumerates them, because they are untracked state that no change carries (twpvqstu). So "is this node drafted?" cannot be a lookup; it is a scan of that directory, and the scan is complete by construction, because landing never deletes a record and nothing a record has said disappears from what the guard reads (twpvqstu). twpvqstu deliberately leaves open which states a caller asks of those records; this node answers it for one caller — removal — by asking for `open`.

The filter is the lifecycle's, not a second list of drafts. `open` and `landed` are the landing fact and its negation and they exhaust it, so "has not landed" is the only condition a not-yet-landed duty can attach to (vkkwusty). Retention is why the filter has to be read rather than assumed: a landed record is kept, so it is present in every later scan and could only be passed over by reading its state, and D7's abandonment would then be withdrawn from any node that had ever been drafted (myprwuxt). Because `landed` is terminal, a record excluded now stays excluded: the guard's answer is stable rather than racing a landing, and the only thing that can clear the refusal is the transition the lifecycle defines (vkkwusty).

Which records are the node's follows from what a record says about a node. A record names exactly one target node, while the handle and not the node is its identity — so the target is a field to compare against the id the caller gave, and the drafts it picks out are named back by handle, the one thing that distinguishes the several drafts of one node (owyntkvw). The same node-independence is why the guard cannot lean on the dependant scan: a record is not a node, is not listed with the nodes and carries no change, so the node set D14 reads has no trace of a draft, and the guard has to read the registry itself (owyntkvw, stnqmzuw). And the registry is one directory for the repository (twpvqstu), so a draft in another workspace is still this node's draft and still blocks: the workspace on a record is a reference, not a boundary (owyntkvw).

Placement in the verb comes from what removal does. Removal abandons the change and releases its owned paths, and the node's own gates go with it; none of that is reversed by a later landing (myprwuxt). A guard asked after the abandonment would therefore be no guard at all — the node the draft names would already be gone — so the record read belongs before the bracket, beside the refusals D14 and D7 already ask there (stnqmzuw, myprwuxt). That is also why the guard is over the id the caller named and not over the gates that follow it: no invocation names those gates, and D7 gives them no guard of their own (myprwuxt). The draft guard is answered after the dependant refusal because D14 fixes that a node with dependants is refused with them named (stnqmzuw), and a guard asked earlier would answer in their place and leave those names unsaid; the cost is a second refusal for a call that must clear both, which is cheaper than a refusal that hides half of what stops it.

Deliberately not here: what a landed record refers to once its target is removed (twpvqstu keeps the record; whether a record's target must still resolve is another question); what the scan does with a record it cannot read, which belongs to the store's own read; whether a draft is ever discarded rather than landed, which the lifecycle provides no transition for (vkkwusty) and this node does not add; any listing or reporting of open drafts, a command surface of its own, and a cap on open records or a barrier that waits on them, both deferred where the lifecycle is fixed (vkkwusty); and how a refusal's lines are worded and rendered, which belongs to the envelope rather than to the guard.
